name: Hippocampal Pattern Separation and Completion
higher_order_principle: The dentate gyrus (DG) performs pattern separation — making similar inputs more distinct to prevent interference. CA3 performs pattern completion — reactivating full stored patterns from partial cues. These two operations are in dynamic tension: too much separation → memories are isolated and don't generalize; too much completion → similar memories interfere and blur together. The balance between separation and completion determines whether similar learning episodes are discriminated or confused.

parameters.mechanism: DG has sparse coding — few neurons active for any given input. Even slightly different inputs activate non-overlapping DG populations. This creates distinct CA3 patterns for similar experiences.
parameters.educational_implication: INTERLEAVING works because DG creates distinct codes for each category exemplar when they appear in varied contexts. BLOCKING fails because DG codes are similar within a block → interference.

parameters.mechanism: CA3 recurrent connections (autoassociative network) allow partial cue to reactivate the complete stored pattern. This is the mechanism of memory retrieval.
parameters.educational_implication: Retrieval practice EXERCISES the pattern completion pathway. Each successful retrieval strengthens the cue → pattern association. This is why testing works: it strengthens the specific neural pathway of retrieval.

parameters.separation_dominant: high discrimination (can distinguish similar items), low generalization (doesn't see connections between similar cases)
parameters.completion_dominant: high generalization (sees patterns across cases), low discrimination (confuses similar items)
parameters.educational_note: Novices need separation (distinguish concept A from concept B). Experts need completion (see the pattern across many examples). Interleaving promotes separation; blocked practice promotes completion. This may explain why interleaving benefits novices more.

scope_conditions: DG neurogenesis (new neurons) supports pattern separation. Aerobic exercise increases neurogenesis → improves separation performance.
Aging degrades DG function → older adults shift towards pattern completion (bias to see things as 'same as before' even when changed).
Stress impairs DG separation → stressed learners confuse similar concepts.
moderators: input_similarity (highly similar inputs demand more separation)

interactions.description: Novelty signal (T17) biases hippocampus towards encoding (separation). Familiarity biases towards retrieval (completion).
E2 describes the internal computational mechanics of E1. E1 is the macro-process; E2 is the micro-circuitry.

key_references: Yassa, M. A., & Stark, C. E. L. (2011). Pattern separation in the hippocampus. Trends in Neurosciences
Leutgeb, J. K., et al. (2007). Pattern separation in the dentate gyrus. Science
Rolls, E. T. (2013). The mechanisms for pattern completion and pattern separation in the hippocampus. Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience
